act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Theft
keywords: theft stolen property stealing robbery shoplifting pickpocket vehicle motorcycle bike stolen
plain_text: Theft is the dishonest taking of movable property out of the possession of any person without consent. Punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both. Aggravated theft (house-breaking, vehicle theft, theft at night) carries higher punishment up to 7 years. File an FIR immediately and note down the serial numbers and description of stolen property.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Robbery
keywords: robbery mugging snatching chain snatching violent theft bag snatched held up dacoity
plain_text: Robbery is theft with the use or threat of force. Punishment: rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and fine. Dacoity (robbery by 5 or more persons) carries up to life imprisonment. File FIR immediately. Preserve any CCTV footage or eyewitness contacts. Robbery is a non-bailable, cognizable offence.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Extortion
keywords: extortion blackmail threat money coercion demand threat harm pay or else ransom
plain_text: Whoever intentionally puts a person in fear of injury and dishonestly induces them to deliver property or valuable security commits extortion. Punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years or fine or both. Threatening online (WhatsApp, calls) also qualifies. Report to police and cybercrime portal. Keep all threatening messages as evidence.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Assault and causing hurt
keywords: assault beating hit punch slap hurt injury physical attack fight neighbour attack hit by someone
plain_text: Voluntarily causing hurt (bodily pain, disease or infirmity) is punishable with imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to Rs. 1000 or both. Grievous hurt (permanent disability, fracture, disfigurement): up to 7 years. Gather medical evidence (hospital records, doctor certificate). File FIR. Photograph injuries immediately.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Assault on woman / Sexual harassment
keywords: sexual harassment molestation outrage modesty woman assault touch inappropriate groping eve teasing
plain_text: Assault or criminal force on a woman intending to outrage her modesty: imprisonment of 1 to 5 years and fine. Sexual harassment at workplace covered under POSH Act 2013. Stalking (BNS Section 78) punishable up to 3 years first offence, 5 years repeat. Report to police; a female officer must record statement. Keep messages and witness details.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Rape
keywords: rape sexual assault sexual violence non consensual sex survivor report
plain_text: Rape: minimum 10 years rigorous imprisonment extendable to life, plus fine. Survivor can report at ANY police station (Zero FIR). A female officer must record statement. Medical examination only with survivor's consent. Identity of survivor must not be disclosed. Free legal aid is available. Contact One-Stop Centres (Sakhi): 7827170170. Limitation: No limitation period for reporting.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Cheating and fraud
keywords: cheating fraud deceive false promise online fraud money scam fake investment job fraud lottery advance fee
plain_text: Cheating by deceiving a person and dishonestly inducing them to deliver property: imprisonment up to 7 years and fine. Online investment fraud, job fraud, advance-fee scams also covered under IT Act Section 66D. Report at cybercrime.gov.in immediately. Freeze the fraud transaction by calling your bank (RBI rule: report within 3 days for zero liability). Keep all payment receipts, messages, and call records.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Criminal intimidation and threats
keywords: threat intimidation threatening harm death injury reputation online threat call threat WhatsApp threat
plain_text: Threatening someone with injury to person, reputation, or property to cause alarm: imprisonment up to 2 years or fine. Threat of death or grievous hurt: up to 7 years. Online threats via WhatsApp, SMS, or call are also cognizable under IT Act. Screenshot threats. Note time and date. File FIR. Request call records from police if the caller is unknown.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Defamation
keywords: defamation reputation false statement slander libel social media post fake news WhatsApp fake message
plain_text: Making or publishing any imputation about a person intending to harm their reputation is defamation. Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years or fine. Truth published for public good is a valid defence. Online defamation (social media, WhatsApp) also attracts IT Act Section 66. Civil defamation suit for damages can be filed separately in civil court. Preserve screenshots of defamatory posts.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Criminal trespass and house-breaking
keywords: trespass enter property without permission break in house break in locked out encroach entering land
plain_text: Criminal trespass: entering property to commit an offence or intimidate occupants — imprisonment up to 3 months or fine or both. House-breaking (breaking into a dwelling): imprisonment up to 2 years. If done at night (lurking house-trespass): up to 3 years. Landlord unlawfully entering tenant's premises also qualifies as trespass. File FIR and note date, time, witnesses.

act: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 / Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973
title: First Information Report (FIR)
keywords: FIR police complaint first information report register complaint police refuse refusal cognizable offence file FIR
plain_text: An FIR is filed for cognizable offences (serious crimes: theft, assault, rape, murder, fraud). Police CANNOT refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence. If refused: (1) Send written complaint by post to SP/DCP with acknowledgement, (2) Approach Executive Magistrate under BNSS Section 175, (3) File complaint directly in court under BNSS Section 223. A free copy of the FIR must be given to the complainant. You can file an FIR at ANY police station (Zero FIR) regardless of jurisdiction.

act: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 / Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973
title: Zero FIR
keywords: zero FIR police station jurisdiction wrong station any police station away from home
plain_text: A Zero FIR can be filed at ANY police station regardless of where the offence occurred or which station has jurisdiction. The receiving station must register it (numbered as Zero FIR) and transfer it to the correct jurisdiction station within 15 days. It is especially useful when a crime occurs away from your home district, you are not sure which station has jurisdiction, or the correct station is refusing to act.

act: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 / Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973
title: Rights upon arrest
keywords: arrest police arrest rights arrest warrant illegally detained custody arrested handcuffed
plain_text: Rights upon arrest: (1) Right to know the grounds of arrest in writing, (2) Right to inform a friend, relative or lawyer of the arrest, (3) Right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice, (4) Right to be produced before Magistrate within 24 hours, (5) Right to bail in bailable offences without delay, (6) Right to free legal aid if unable to afford a lawyer, (7) Right to remain silent (statements to police are not admissible as confessions). Illegal detention or custodial violence: file Habeas Corpus petition in High Court.

act: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 / Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) 1973
title: Anticipatory Bail
keywords: anticipatory bail arrest fear bail before arrest pre arrest bail apprehension arrest non bailable
plain_text: If a person fears arrest for a non-bailable offence, they can apply to Sessions Court or High Court for anticipatory bail. If granted, police must release them on bail if arrested. Application must state: grounds of apprehension, previous criminal record (if any), willingness to cooperate with investigation. Police can oppose it. Court may impose conditions. Apply BEFORE arrest. This does not prevent police from questioning you.

act: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023 / CrPC 1973
title: Bail and remand rights
keywords: bail remand custody police custody judicial custody bail application bailable non-bailable magistrate
plain_text: After arrest, police can hold a person for up to 24 hours and must produce them before a Magistrate. Magistrate can grant judicial remand (up to 15 days at a time) or bail. In bailable offences, bail is a right — police must grant it. In non-bailable offences, only a Magistrate/court can grant bail. Default bail (also called statutory bail) is available if chargesheet is not filed in 60 days (serious offences) or 90 days (offences punishable with death/life) from the date of arrest.

act: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
title: Domestic Violence — Protection, Residence and Monetary Orders
keywords: domestic violence husband wife family abuse physical emotional verbal financial dowry beating in laws marital cruelty
plain_text: Any woman in a domestic relationship facing physical, sexual, verbal, emotional, or economic abuse can approach a Magistrate for: (1) Protection Order — prohibiting abuser from committing further violence, (2) Residence Order — right to remain in the shared household, (3) Monetary Relief — maintenance, medical expenses, and loss of earnings, (4) Custody Order — temporary custody of children, (5) Compensation Order. File application before Magistrate with help of a Protection Officer (at every district). FIR can also be filed under BNS/IPC Section 498A (cruelty by husband and relatives). Both civil and criminal remedies can be pursued simultaneously.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860
title: Cruelty by husband or relatives (Dowry harassment)
keywords: dowry harassment dowry demand cruelty husband in-laws torture 498A mental cruelty wife harassment
plain_text: Cruelty by husband or relatives including dowry demands, mental or physical harassment is a cognizable, non-bailable criminal offence. Punishment: up to 3 years imprisonment and fine. File FIR at local police station. Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 also applies — demanding or giving dowry is punishable with minimum 6 months imprisonment. Stridhan (woman's personal gifts and property) must be returned on demand. Preserve all evidence of demands: messages, witnesses, medical records.

act: Consumer Protection Act 2019
title: Consumer Rights and Consumer Commission
keywords: consumer complaint defective product bad service online shopping refund cheated purchased goods services e-commerce amazon flipkart
plain_text: A consumer can file complaint for defective goods, deficient service, unfair trade practice, or misleading advertisement. Forums (based on claim amount): District Commission (up to Rs. 50 lakh), State Commission (Rs. 50 lakh to Rs. 2 crore), National Commission (above Rs. 2 crore). File online at edaakhil.nic.in or consumerhelpline.gov.in (helpline: 1800-11-4000). No lawyer needed for District Commission. Limitation: 2 years from cause of action. E-commerce companies are also liable. Remedies: refund, replacement, compensation, punitive damages.

act: Consumer Protection Act 2019
title: Consumer definitions and e-commerce rights
keywords: consumer definition service deficiency defective product warranty guarantee online shopping ecommerce return refund reject
plain_text: Consumer: anyone who buys goods or hires services for personal use (not for commercial resale). Includes online purchases. E-commerce platform liability: sellers and platforms both can be held responsible for defective products. Manufacturers also liable under product liability provisions. Complaint can be filed in the state where the consumer resides, not where the company is located. Mediation is available for quick resolution before full hearing.

act: Transfer of Property Act 1882 / Rent Control Acts (State-specific)
title: Landlord-Tenant — Eviction, notice, and rights
keywords: landlord tenant eviction notice rent house locked out illegal eviction security deposit lock change electricity cut water cut
plain_text: Landlord CANNOT evict a tenant without proper notice and a court order. Required notice: 15 days for month-to-month tenancy, 6 months for annual tenancy. Forceful eviction, locking premises, cutting electricity/water without court order is ILLEGAL and constitutes criminal trespass. Tenant's remedies: (1) FIR for illegal eviction under BNS Section 329 (criminal trespass), (2) Application to Rent Controller, (3) Civil suit for injunction. Rent agreement (even unregistered) is valid evidence. Security deposit must be returned with interest as per state law.

act: Registration Act 1908 / Transfer of Property Act 1882
title: Property sale, registration, and title
keywords: property sale land registration title document sale deed property fraud benami property cheated on property
plain_text: Any sale of immovable property valued above Rs. 100 must be registered. An unregistered sale deed does not transfer legal title. Before buying property: verify title through registered documents at Sub-Registrar office, check encumbrance certificate for loans or legal disputes, verify mutation records at Tehsil/Panchayat. Property fraud (fake documents, double selling): file FIR under BNS Section 318 (cheating) and BNS Section 336 (forgery). Benami property (in someone else's name) is illegal under Benami Transactions Act 1988.

act: Indian Contract Act 1872
title: Contract — validity, breach, and remedies
keywords: contract agreement breach promise broken deal signed agreement not paid refund service not provided verbal agreement
plain_text: Valid contract requires: offer + acceptance, consideration (payment/value), free consent (no coercion, fraud, or undue influence), lawful purpose, and competent parties (age 18+). Breach: if one party fails to perform, the other can claim actual losses (Section 73). Unlawful contracts (illegal, immoral, against public policy) are void and unenforceable. A contract with a minor (under 18) is completely void. Oral contracts are valid but hard to prove — prefer written agreements. Limitation to file civil suit for contract breach: 3 years.

act: Specific Relief Act 1963
title: Specific performance of contract
keywords: specific performance force other party to honour agreement property sale contract not honoured land deal breach
plain_text: When a seller refuses to transfer property despite taking advance payment, the buyer can file a suit for specific performance — asking the court to force the seller to complete the transaction. Available for property sales, unique goods, and contracts where money compensation is not adequate. Must be filed within 3 years of the breach. An interim injunction can prevent the seller from selling to anyone else during the case. File suit in civil court having jurisdiction over the property.

act: Information Technology Act 2000 and Amendment 2008
title: Cybercrime — Hacking, identity theft, online fraud
keywords: hacking cyber crime phishing identity theft OTP fraud online fraud fake account social media hack password stolen account hacked
plain_text: Key cyber offences: Section 66 (hacking/computer damage — up to 3 years), Section 66C (identity theft using another's password/OTP — up to 3 years), Section 66D (impersonation online — up to 3 years), Section 67 (obscene material — up to 5 years). Report: cybercrime.gov.in or nearest Cybercrime police station. For financial fraud: immediately call your bank and report to RBI Ombudsman. Freeze transaction within 3 days for zero-liability protection. Preserve screenshots, emails, transaction IDs.

act: Information Technology Act 2000 / IT Rules 2021
title: Non-consensual intimate image sharing (Revenge porn / Morphed images)
keywords: private photos videos leaked revenge porn morphed images intimate images shared without consent deepfake nude fake image
plain_text: Sharing private intimate images without consent: IT Act Section 66E (violation of privacy — up to 3 years and Rs. 2 lakh fine), Section 67/67A (obscene/sexually explicit material — up to 5 years). BNS Section 79 (voyeurism) also applies. Morphed/deepfake images using AI are also covered. Social media platforms must remove such content within 24 hours of reporting. File complaint at cybercrime.gov.in and local police. Request an emergency ex-parte injunction in court to stop further spread.

act: Information Technology Act 2000 / IT Rules 2021
title: Data privacy and data breach
keywords: data breach personal data leaked privacy violation company leaked my data data misuse Aadhaar data stolen
plain_text: Companies handling sensitive personal data (passwords, financial, health information) must protect it under IT Act Section 43A. Negligent data breach causing wrongful loss: compensation claim against the company. Misuse of personal information by a company employee (Section 72A): imprisonment up to 3 years and fine. Report data breach to CERT-In. File complaint with company's DPO (Data Protection Officer). In case of Aadhaar misuse, report to UIDAI at 1947.

act: Right to Information Act 2005 (RTI)
title: RTI — Right to Government Information
keywords: RTI right to information government document transparency application public authority record file status government document
plain_text: Any citizen can request information from any public authority (government department, PSU, local body, court registries, etc.). How to file: write to Public Information Officer (PIO), pay Rs. 10 fee (BPL applicants exempt). Online: rtionline.gov.in. Response time: 30 days (48 hours if life/liberty at stake). If PIO refuses or delays: First Appeal to First Appellate Authority (within 30 days), then Second Appeal to Central or State Information Commission. PIO can be penalized Rs. 250/day (up to Rs. 25,000) for delay. RTI cannot access personal privacy information or national security matters.

act: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and Amendment 2019
title: Road accident — compensation, hit and run, insurance
keywords: road accident car accident hit and run vehicle accident injury death compensation insurance claim MACT motor accident
plain_text: Immediate duty after accident: stop, help injured, report to nearest police station and inform insurance company. Hit and run: victims get compensation from Solatium Fund (Rs. 25,000 for grievous hurt, Rs. 2 lakh for death). Compensation from insurer: file before Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT). No-fault liability (Section 164): Rs. 5 lakh for death, Rs. 2.5 lakh for permanent disability — no need to prove negligence. Fault liability: higher compensation based on income, age, and negligence. Limitation: 6 months to file accident claim (can be extended). Driving without insurance: imprisonment up to 3 months and fine.

act: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012 (POCSO)
title: Child Sexual Abuse — POCSO
keywords: child abuse sexual abuse minor child molestation POCSO child pornography child exploitation under 18
plain_text: POCSO protects children (under 18) from sexual assault, sexual harassment, and child pornography. All offences: cognizable, non-bailable, with special courts. Reporting is MANDATORY for anyone with knowledge (failure to report: punishment up to 6 months). Child-friendly procedure: statement at home or comfort place, no repeated questioning, in-camera trial, support person allowed. Report: police or CHILDLINE 1098. Accused is presumed guilty (reverse burden of proof). Penetrative sexual assault: minimum 10 years to life.

act: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989
title: Atrocities against SC/ST — Rights and Procedures
keywords: caste discrimination SC ST atrocity untouchability caste abuse humiliation dalit land grab social boycott caste slur
plain_text: Intentional insult, intimidation, land grabbing, forced labour, social boycott, or caste-based abuse against SC/ST members is a cognizable, non-bailable offence. Special SC/ST courts handle these cases. Victim entitled to compensation, immediate relief (food, shelter, travel), and rehabilitation. DSP-level officer must personally investigate. Bail is harder for the accused to obtain. Anticipatory bail is generally not available to accused in SC/ST Atrocities cases. Government must provide legal aid to the victim.

act: Industrial Disputes Act 1947 / Payment of Wages Act 1936 / Code on Wages 2019
section: ID Act Section 25F, 25G, 25N; Wages Act Section 3, 4, 5
title: Labour rights — Wrongful termination and unpaid wages
keywords: fired job terminated dismissed wrongful termination salary not paid dues not cleared unpaid wages labor retrenchment layoff
plain_text: Employer cannot retrench a permanent worker (100+ workers establishment) without: 3 months notice/pay, retrenchment compensation (15 days wages per year of service), government permission. Unpaid wages: complaint to Labour Commissioner or Authority under Code on Wages within 3 years. Wrongful dismissal: approach Labour Court for reinstatement and back wages. Standing Orders must be followed. Forced resignation (under pressure): may be treated as wrongful termination. Preserve offer letter, salary slips, appointment letter, and any termination notice.

act: Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1952
title: PF — Provident Fund rights
keywords: PF provident fund EPF EPFO employer not depositing PF deducted not paid gratuity PF withdrawal
plain_text: Employer must deposit both employee's and employer's share of PF (12% each) to EPFO. Non-deposit of PF despite deducting from salary is a criminal offence (Section 14). Complaint: EPFO regional office or file online at epfigms.gov.in (helpline 1800-118-005). Employer withholding gratuity (Payment of Gratuity Act 1972): entitlement after 5 continuous years — file complaint with Controlling Authority. PF withdrawal: apply online through UAN portal. Limitation to file PF case: no strict limitation (file as soon as possible).

act: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881
title: Cheque bounce
keywords: cheque bounce dishonoured cheque returned cheque insufficient funds bounced cheque loan repayment stop payment
plain_text: Cheque bouncing for insufficient funds or other reasons: payee must send written legal notice within 30 days of receiving cheque return memo. Drawer has 15 days from notice to pay. If unpaid, file criminal complaint in court within 30 days after the 15-day notice period expires. Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years or twice the cheque amount, or both. This is compoundable (can be settled). Also file civil suit for recovery. Total window from cheque return to court filing: 75 days. Do not miss any deadline — it will bar your claim permanently.

act: Code of Civil Procedure 1908 / Specific Relief Act 1963
section: CPC Order 39 Rule 1–2; Specific Relief Act Section 38, 39
title: Civil injunction — Emergency court order
keywords: injunction stop court order restrain someone civil court property dispute construction encroachment demolish urgent court order
plain_text: When someone is about to take an action that will cause irreversible harm (demolishing your property, taking your assets, encroaching land), you can apply for a temporary injunction (stay order) in civil court. The court can pass an ex-parte (emergency, one-sided) injunction the same day in urgent cases. Three conditions must be met: (1) Prima facie case in your favour, (2) Balance of convenience in your favour, (3) Irreparable harm if injunction not granted. File a civil suit along with injunction application. Limitation for injunction: same as the underlying civil suit (3–12 years depending on nature).

act: Constitution of India
title: Fundamental Rights — Liberty, writs, and remedies
keywords: fundamental rights personal liberty illegal detention habeas corpus writ petition high court supreme court government violation arrest illegal
plain_text: Article 21: Right to life and personal liberty — cannot be taken away except by law. Article 22: Protection against arbitrary arrest (right to know grounds, right to lawyer, produced before Magistrate in 24 hours). Article 32: Right to approach Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. Article 226: Right to approach High Court for any legal right violation. Writ types: Habeas Corpus (illegal detention), Mandamus (force authority to perform duty), Certiorari (quash illegal order), Prohibition (stop lower authority), Quo Warranto (challenge appointment). Police brutality and custodial violence are violations of Article 21.

act: Limitation Act 1963
title: Limitation periods — Deadlines to file cases
keywords: limitation period deadline time limit file case expired missed deadline court case how long time barred
plain_text: KEY LIMITATION PERIODS: Contract disputes — 3 years from breach. Property recovery (possession) — 12 years. Money due on contract — 3 years. Consumer forum — 2 years from cause of action. Cheque bounce — 1 month from expiry of 15-day notice period. FIR — no limitation for serious crimes. Accident/tort — 3 years. Limitation can be extended for fraud (Section 17), mistake (Section 18), or disability (Section 6). MISSING A DEADLINE permanently bars the claim in most cases. File court application immediately if deadline is close. Court can condone delay for sufficient cause (Section 5) — apply with reasons.

act: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987
title: Free legal aid — NALSA and DLSA
keywords: free legal aid lawyer poor no money legal help DLSA SLSA legal services authority NALSA 15100 free lawyer
plain_text: FREE LEGAL AID is a constitutional right (Article 39A). Who is eligible: annual income below Rs. 3 lakh (Central), women, children, SC/ST, disabled, industrial workers, victims of disaster or trafficking, persons in custody. How to apply: go to District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at every district court, or call NALSA Helpline: 15100. They provide free lawyers, legal advice, mediation, Lok Adalat referral. Lok Adalat (Section 20): settles disputes amicably — award is a decree and is final. Mobile Legal Aid Clinics also available in rural areas.

act: Indian Evidence Act 1872 / Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023
title: Evidence — Electronic evidence and admissibility
keywords: evidence proof electronic evidence screenshot WhatsApp message email video CCTV admissible court call recording certificate
plain_text: Electronic evidence (screenshots, WhatsApp messages, emails, call recordings, CCTV footage) is admissible in court under Section 65B. REQUIREMENT: produce a Section 65B certificate from the device owner/custodian certifying that the electronic record was produced accurately. Preserve original devices — do not delete or alter digital evidence. Screenshots must show timestamps, sender IDs, and context. Confession to police is NOT admissible. Confession made freely before a Magistrate IS admissible. Evidence tampered or fabricated is itself an offence. Chain of custody must be maintained for physical evidence.

act: Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 / BNS 2023
title: Dowry — Prohibition, demand, and dowry death
keywords: dowry demand marriage jewelry gold money in-laws husband family demand gifts dowry death murder bride burning
plain_text: Giving or taking dowry is illegal. Demanding dowry: minimum 6 months, maximum 2 years imprisonment and fine of Rs. 10,000 or value of dowry (whichever is more). Stridhan (wife's own property and gifts received at or after marriage) belongs solely to the wife and must be returned on demand. Dowry death (BNS Section 80): if a woman dies within 7 years of marriage due to burns, injury, or suspicious circumstances connected to dowry demands, the presumption of dowry death arises against husband and in-laws (punishable with 7 years to life imprisonment). Preserve all evidence of dowry demands: messages, witnesses, videos, transfer records.

act: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013 (POSH Act)
title: Workplace sexual harassment (POSH)
keywords: sexual harassment workplace office boss colleague POSH ICC internal complaint committee unwanted advances quid pro quo hostile environment
plain_text: Every employer with 10+ employees MUST have an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC). Unorganized sector employers must report to Local Complaints Committee (LCC) at district level. Complaint must be filed within 3 months of incident (extendable to 6 months for sufficient reason). ICC inquiry: must be completed within 90 days. Remedies: warning, salary deduction, termination of harasser, compensation. False complaints also punishable. Types covered: quid pro quo (demand for favours) and hostile work environment. Complaint is strictly confidential. If employer has no ICC, it is itself an offence. Police FIR is also an option simultaneously.

act: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007
title: Senior citizen rights — Maintenance and property transfer
keywords: old parents elderly abandoned maintenance children support senior citizen property transfer neglect parents nursing home
plain_text: Adult children and grandchildren are legally obligated to maintain parents/grandparents who cannot support themselves. Application to Maintenance Tribunal (Sub-Divisional Magistrate): maintenance up to Rs. 10,000/month (some states higher). Property transfer reversal (Section 23): if parents transferred property to a child who then neglects them, the transfer can be declared VOID. Abandoning senior citizens (in hospitals, pilgrimages, etc.) is a criminal offence. Each state has a Senior Citizens Helpline (Elderline: 14567). Complaint can also be filed with district Social Welfare Officer.

act: Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 (PMLA)
title: Money laundering
keywords: money laundering black money corruption bribe shell company property bought from illegal money Enforcement Directorate ED
plain_text: Money laundering is the process of converting proceeds of crime into apparently legitimate assets. It is a cognizable, non-bailable offence investigated by the Enforcement Directorate (ED). Punishment: rigorous imprisonment 3–7 years (up to 10 years in some cases) and fine. Reporting entities (banks, financial institutions) must report suspicious transactions to Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU). If you have received funds or property from a person you believe may be engaged in crime, seek immediate legal advice. Bribing a public official is separately punishable under Prevention of Corruption Act 1988.

act: Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 / Lokpal and Lokayukta Act 2013
title: Bribery and corruption
keywords: bribe government official corrupt police officer bribery demand money for service government work public servant
plain_text: Giving or taking a bribe to or by a public servant is a criminal offence. Bribe-giver punishment: up to 7 years and fine. Bribe-taker punishment: minimum 3 years, up to 7 years and fine. How to report: Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) of your state (most have online complaint portals), Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) at cvc.gov.in for central government employees, Lokpal (central) or Lokayukta (state). You can set a trap with ACB: approach them with evidence of demand and they will conduct a sting. Whistleblower Protection Act 2014 protects persons reporting corruption.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 / IPC 1860
title: Forgery of documents
keywords: forged document fake document false signature fake signature property forgery fake deed forged cheque
plain_text: Forgery: making a false document with intent to cause damage or injury to the public or any person. Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years and fine. Forgery of valuable security, will, or authority: up to 7 years. Using a forged document: same punishment as making it. Common examples: forged property deeds, fake educational certificates, forged cheques. File FIR and preserve original documents and any expert handwriting/stamp comparison evidence. Expert opinion on documents can be obtained from government-approved forensic labs.

act: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023
title: Stalking
keywords: stalking following watching monitoring online stalking cyber stalking ex partner harassment track location
plain_text: Stalking (following, contacting, or monitoring a woman against her will): imprisonment up to 3 years for first offence, up to 5 years for subsequent offence. Online stalking (monitoring social media, tracking device, hacking email/phone) is also covered. Women stalking men: covered under civil harassment laws and IT Act. Preserve: records of all contacts, screenshots of messages, call logs. File FIR under BNS Section 78. Court can issue restraining order. In urgent cases, approach court for an ex-parte injunction.

act: Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC)
title: Executing a court decree — Recovering a judgment debt
keywords: court decree execution recovery money awarded not paying decree holder judgment enforcement attachment
plain_text: After winning a court case, if the other party refuses to pay the decreed amount: file an Execution Petition in the same court that passed the decree. Court can: attach and sell the debtor's property or bank accounts, arrest and detain the debtor (for certain types of decrees), appoint a receiver. Execution must be filed within 12 years of the decree. If the other party has transferred property to avoid payment, file a suit for fraudulent transfer (Section 53 Transfer of Property Act). Bank account attachment is the fastest recovery method — provide the court with the debtor's bank details.

act: Hindu Succession Act 1956 / Indian Succession Act 1925
section: Hindu Succession Act Section 6, 8, 15, 16; ISA Section 32, 63
title: Inheritance and succession rights
keywords: inheritance will property death father died mother died succession property share siblings excluded from property
plain_text: Hindu inheritance (Hindu Succession Act): daughters have equal coparcenary rights in ancestral property as sons (Amendment 2005). A wife inherits along with children as Class I heirs. Making a Will: any adult of sound mind can make a will. For Hindus, will must be signed and witnessed by two witnesses. Registered will is stronger evidence. Without a will (intestate): property divided equally among Class I heirs. Challenging a will: file probate petition or suit for declaration of invalidity within 12 years. Muslims: governed by Muslim Personal Law (1/3 can be bequeathed; rest per Shariat). Christians: Indian Succession Act 1925.

act: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 / Special Marriage Act 1954
title: Marriage — Divorce, maintenance, and matrimonial rights
keywords: divorce separation maintenance alimony husband wife marital dispute marriage dissolution custody children
plain_text: Grounds for divorce (Hindu): cruelty, adultery, desertion (2 years), conversion, mental illness, leprosy, venereal disease, renunciation, presumed death. Mutual consent divorce: both parties agree, file petition, 6-month cooling period (court may waive). Maintenance (Section 24): either spouse can claim interim maintenance during divorce proceedings. Permanent alimony (Section 25): court may award lump sum or monthly payment based on income and assets. Restitution of conjugal rights (Section 9): court can direct deserting spouse to return. Custody of children: court decides based on child's best interest. Jurisdiction: court in area where parties last resided together.

act: Guardians and Wards Act 1890 / Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956
title: Child custody and guardianship
keywords: custody children divorce child custody visitation rights guardian minor child welfare parental kidnapping
plain_text: After separation or divorce, custody of children is decided by the court based solely on the child's welfare and best interest. Natural guardian: for a Hindu boy or unmarried girl below 5 years, the mother is the natural guardian. For older children, the father is natural guardian (but court can override this). A child above 9 years: court considers child's own preference. Parental child abduction (taking child without court order): FIR under BNS Section 137/138 (kidnapping). Interim custody orders: file application in family court for immediate custody. International child abduction: Hague Convention (India is not a signatory but courts exercise jurisdiction).

act: Environment Protection Act 1986 / National Green Tribunal Act 2010
title: Environmental violations and NGT
keywords: pollution factory noise pollution air pollution water pollution illegal mining environmental damage dumping waste NGT
plain_text: Any person or group of persons can approach the National Green Tribunal (NGT) for environmental violations: illegal pollution, noise nuisance, damage to forests or water bodies. No filing fee for public interest matters. NGT can award compensation, order restoration, and direct closure of offending unit. State Pollution Control Boards receive complaints about industries violating pollution norms. Noise pollution (Noise Pollution Rules 2000): complaint to local police or District Magistrate. Illegal construction in eco-sensitive zones: complaint to State Environment Impact Assessment Authority.
